newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Late N.Korean leader's distant kin defects.
newsitem.headline: Late N.Korean leader's distant kin defects.

text.p: Two North Korean families, including a distant relative of the Stalinist state's late leader Kim Il-sung, defected to South Korea by sea on Wednesday, the state Agency for National Security Planning said.
An agency statement said two families of four sought political asylum after entering South Korean waters in the Yellow Sea between China and the Korean peninsula.
Among the eight was Kim Young-jin, a relative by marriage to Kim Il-sung's wife, it said.
The defectors, rescued by South Korean maritime police, were due to arrive at the port of Inchon, just west of Seoul, at around 7:00 p.m. (1000 GMT).

The agency did not give any further details, but Yonhap television news earlier reported they made the journey in freezing winter temperatures in a small boat and were being brought to Inchon on a patrol vessel.
An increasing number of North Koreans have fled the country and sought asylum in the South following several years of chronic food shortages in the North.

Last month, a family of 16 and a security guard, the largest group of North Korean defectors since the 1950-53 Korean War, arrived in Seoul six weeks after launching an epic escape through China and Hong Kong.
The 17 later told a news conference that the impoverished North had nearly tripled the guards along its borders with China and Russia to stop escapes.
They also said North Koreans had been advised to prepare for possible chemical, biological and nuclear warfare by making and keeping at home clothes and devices to protect themselves.
The recent increase in defections has been a propaganda coup for South Korea but has also brought worries about how Seoul would cope if the flights became a surge of refugee from the communist North.
The two Koreas remain technically at war because their conflict ended in a truce and not a peace agreement.
